From the terrifying first trailer to the scathing reviews, I knew at some point in my life I was going to watch Cats. It was too much of an anomaly, too high-budget a disaster for me to ignore, I didn’t want to watch it, I HAD to see just how bad it was. And fuck me was this an absolutely terrifying fever dream filled with an uncomfortable amount of drugs, sex and music without having any drugs or sex and too much music. I’m genuinely scarred for having seen it all the way through. Let’s start with the plot. There isn’t any. And I’m not just saying that to be funny, this entire film is 90 minutes of introductions, 10 minutes of actual story and the other 10 minutes is weird panting and gyrating. Here I’ll give you a rundown of what happens; we open with our lead Victoria being abandoned by her owners, she’s introduced to the Jellicle Cats with their Jellicle Ball – and sidenote, they never explain what a Jellicle is and why it’s important to be one despite them saying Jellicle about 587 fucking times in the first five minutes – who take her to see the cats hoping to become the Jellicle choice and live a new life in the fucking sky or something. I swear to Christ, the little plot I can recognise as a story makes me think this is about a fucking suicide cult. From there Victoria meets Rebel Wilson’s hairy cooch, Jason Derulo’s CGI bulge, James Corden’s fat arse, a couple thieving twins who I couldn’t tell if they were related or not because of the fuck me eyes they were flashing at each other, Judi Dench’s old face and Ian McKellen making Meow noises before we actually get to the Jellicle Ball in which the contestants are STILL being introduced since the bad guy – Idris Elba and his unnervingly smooth fur body – has been stealing all the contestants with magic – oh by the way there’s fucking MAGIC in this film, they kinda dropped that on you without warning – so anyone who’s still taking part in the Ball we’ve never fucking seen before, making their musical numbers an exercise in futility because I don’t know them and I don’t want to fucking know them. Those two paragraphs cover around 80% of the story, all this film has is cats introducing themselves through song for an hour and a fucking half and then getting lucky if they have anything to say afterwards. It’s not a plot, it’s a fucking 2 hour montage of people we’ve never seen before and it doesn’t stop, new characters are still being introduced with their own numbers with over half the film already done. The only time it actually works is with Mr Mistoffelees who, despite a fairly low amount of screen-time, has been shown to be a cowardly magician and needs confidence to do Big Magic, that works but it comes so late into the game that it couldn’t save the rest of this train wreck. And before anyone dares defend this film, I know it’s based on a musical and I know it’s a different medium, but Hamilton managed to tell an entire historical story with only singing, this is just cats singing about themselves without a story to give them a reason to sing about themselves. The cast is absolutely stacked with big names who are given nothing to work with, and the ones that have something are the weakest actors in the film, I feel kinda bad for Francesca Hayward who plays Victoria because she’s suppose to be our lead, our surrogate into this bizarre, fucked up world of the Jellicle Cats and she’s given nothing, out of all the speaking parts she has probably the fewest amount of lines, every face she makes has this big wondrous smile about EVERYTHING, no matter how benign, and sure she dances well but in a film where everyone is dancing that doesn’t stand out. This is Hayward’s big theatrical break and she’s the most forgettable element in the film, which ironically might save her career. Out of everyone Victoria meets during the many MANY introductions she has to suffer through, not one of them make it worthwhile to sit through their number. Jason Derolo  - who I just hate in general anyway – sings about how Rum Tum Tugger  is a fussy little cunt then screams for milk, Mungojerrie and Rumpleteazer were the thieving twins who looked like they wanted to do a furry version of a Bratty Sis video, and I didn’t know they were twins until writing this review so that just knocks the film even lower for me. There was also a tap dancing train conductor who serves no fucking purpose, Ray WInstone hissing and wondering where the fuck his career has gone and Taylor Swift who even in a film filled with unnecessary sexual energy, gave off too much sexual energy. Seriously man, I got Lola Bunny flashbacks during her number. Worst of the lot was Rebel Wilson and James Corden as Jennyanyfots and Bustopher Jones respectively, I already dislike these two before going into the film and having them both talk the most out of almost any other character was a kick in the fucking dick. Wilson’s introduction was this disturbing piece where she did the most unsexy sexy poses while the camera focussed on her naked hairy body before bringing in singing mice and marching cockroaches with human faces which Jenny proceeds to eat several of when she’s not singing. Corden meanwhile sings for five minutes about being a fat fuck and eating a lot, that’s the entirety of his character, he’s fucking fat, and the fact that both of them are just allowed to skit and makes shitty jokes is simultaneously distracting from the actual plot while adding nothing to the plot either. Both of them were just playing themselves in fur suits and like I said I think both are fucking overdone anyway so I didn’t give a shit about them either way. The only people I see coming out of here unscathed are Ian McKellen and Judi Dench who both have strong enough careers to look past this blip, although Dench’s monologue at the end where she looks at the camera goes on WAY too long about how a cat is not a dog (the fuck?) and every pause makes you think that it’s finally over but no, she keeps fucking going. Jennifer Hudson as Grizabella should also be ok, despite being important to the film she only has three scenes but among those three is her version of the famous ‘Memories’ number which is unironically good, hell I’d say too good for this turd of a film. I’m also hoping that Idris Elba comes out of this unaffected, his villain Macavity is suitably villainous and his motivations generically evil enough – he wants to be the Jellicle Choice because Fuck You I guess – that Elba can work something out with the material but between nobody being able to recognise the most wanted cat in town and his own horrifying nude cat-body, I doubt he’s getting away from this thing clean. Director Tom Hooper has done a few things of note over the last few years, namely his last three films were all Oscar winners and he brought Les Mes to the big screen so I can see why he’s be chosen for this. But holy hell does he fuck this up, this has to go down as one of the biggest fuck-ups of direction of the 21st Century because while Hooper doesn’t do anything technically wrong, nothing he does is done right. Let’s get the big one out of the way; the cats look fucking weird, I knew the cats looked weird, I saw the trailer, I saw the memes, but nothing prepared me for the seeing them in full CGI horror, the first time I saw a Cat-Man clamber down a brick wall, looking like a human being contorting their body into some kind of fucking Cronenberg nightmare with a tail I realised that this was so much worse than I thought it was going to be. It’s the deepest level of the uncanny valley I’ve seen since The Rock in The Mummy Returns and that was 18 fucking years before this, nobody looks human but they don’t look like a cat either, they’re a disgusting hybrid of the two, these vaguely human looking faces pasted onto what looks like skin-tight cat-suits made with actual cat flesh, it NEVER sits right with you. What makes it even more uncomfortable is that there seems to be no rhyme of reason to the clothing, a few cats wear clothing but most of them are nude and some of them even take off their clothes making them nude and I’m left wondering if this is just a nudist colony with lax rules or if everyone is suppose to be naked and we’re just suppose to accept it. I know I shouldn’t be this focussed on naked cat people but I can’t help it, this movie has forces naked cat people into my fucking brain and given me no fucking logic about why they’re naked, hell I haven’t even touched upon the Rebel Wilson scene where she unzips her naked fur-body, as  in literally takes off her skin, to reveal a dance outfit underneath. It’s the tightness as well, I don’t know why they went out of their way to make the cats sexy but it just feels wrong, all the naked cat actors have all their curves pronounced so that every breast, every bulge, every butt covered in fur is on full display but without any form of genitals. Elba gets the worst of it because his fur colour is identical to his skin colour leaving him looking like a fucking Ken Doll with ears but not one person looks good like this. And that’s not even talking about how horny this film is, I heard the stories, I read the reviews that talked about how sexual the film was but it’s not until you’re seeing this cat people twist their bodies together, panting in unison and nuzzle into each other that you have to take a step back and realise that humans doing cat actions is trying way too hard to be sexy whilst not trying to be sexy. The Jellicle Ball is the most horrific example, it’s the hissing, the panting, the Judi Dench hairy leg spread, I honestly couldn’t tell you if the film was trying to be this sexual and went way too far or if it wasn’t trying at all and just came off that way by accident. I haven’t even touched upon the fucking music because I don’t know how to, the visual disaster overpowers the audio so much that I can’t tell if anyone actual sung during this film or not. Ok, over exaggeration, a few songs worked but only a few, the aforementioned Memories hit well and I was fine with the Mr Mistoffelees number but outside of them I really can’t remember any of the songs being any good. The opening introduction to the Jellicle Cats was upbeat I guess, I was too distracted by the CONSTANT use of Jellicle, Jennyanydots was too distracting with the human cockroaches and under-skin dress change for me to even remember what the song was. Tugger and Bustopher were both boring, end of discussion, McKellen’s small number as Gus felt like a lot of build-up for a limp-dick crescendo and Swift’s piece of Macavity trying to big him up almost worked as a villain song if I wasn’t distracted by the complete lack of Idris Elba penis. Before this film the only knowledge I had of Cats was hearing Memories here and there and the rape story from Team America, having now seen this film I know even less about Cats and I don’t want to know anything more about Cats. This is one of the strangest, most confusing, unsettling and fucked up pieces of cinema I’ve ever seen that wasn’t an intentional horror movie, I’ve never seen anything like Cats so 10/10 for uniqueness but just because nobody’s done it before doesn’t mean it’s a good idea and Cats the Movie was not a good idea. There’s no story, all we have is oversexed sexless Cat People introducing themselves for 2 hours before nothing happens and the film ends, nobody looks good, only a couple sound good, the CGI is a mess, the sexiness uncomfortable, the songs forgettable and the whole experience traumatising. I’d say you have to see it just to get the full picture yourself but honestly you’re safer avoiding this. 2/10

I watched this film three times in theatres. It was my sophomore year of high school and one of the first films I saw when the theatres reopened. Snowbanks piled outside of the theatre, making those tall industrial lampposts seem small by comparison. I begged my friends to join me to watch this film—, which I had been raving about. Not because I thought it was technically apt, not by any stretch would I make such an argument now or then. No, because I found it hypnotic. We ascended the crusted snowbanks and into the theatre. The final viewing there was only six people in the theatre. My two friends and I, and three grown men in the very back row. For the first twenty minutes or so they meowed at us, and naturally we meowed back. By the end of the film I was overcome by what I can only describe as a psychedelic euphoria. My friends and I, as well as the men danced in front of the theatre screen together—, meowing along to the music. We never spoke a word to those men, I don’t think we ever clearly saw their faces, only backlit silhouettes only further eroded by the joy of human connection. This is a moment that will flash before my eyes on my death bed. This is the high I will forever chase and nothing will ever compare. This is why I love Cats.

Truly demented choices were made. Parts of this work SO well (the moments where they just Dance; Ian McKellen as Gus the Theatre Cat, the Skimbleshanks number; Francesca Hayward's grace, Jennifer Hudson wringing every bit out of "Memory"). Then there's modern 2019 people trying to make sense of a musical revue from the 80s which was based on poems from 1939; so many of the references are incomprehensible to a modern audience to begin with, which leads to shameless mugging and additional jokes because the base material gives them nothing to work with. I love Rebel Wilson ordinarily, but she is not well-served here in the slightest. And most of the original poems are in third-person, the musical makes them sometimes into first-person with the cats often singing about themselves and their own characteristics; they made the wise choice to elevate Victoria to a cat new to the scene, to be the one being explained to in lieu of the stage audience, but then that leaves the final scene where Dame Judi Dench explains what cats are directly to the camera. Judi was intended to be Grizabella in the original West End show and had to drop out due to injury, so it's a nice touch that they gender-bent Old Deuteronomy so she could be in this now as a legacy moment, but her voice is not really up to the material any more, and the faux-elevation of the banal material does not give her sprechstimme any chance for gravitas. The Taylor Swift-written song is hilariously "okay boomer" in response to Memory. Then the design goes uncanny valley, you never know what size anyone is, they sing about things that are not evident on screen (e.g. Macavity being described as a ginger cat when he is the color of Idris Elba), they are often difficult to even look at. The highs and lows combined make this a jaw-dropping must-watch.

My review of Cats (or A Stoner's Journey Into The Heart of Darkness) DISCLAIMER : This review is in no way an endorsement of the movie, please view at your own risk. (Mild Spoilers Ahead) So I finally find did something I had been considering for some time now. I got high and watched Cats and it nearly broke me. To preface, the choice to watch this movie on that very nigjt wasn't exactly random. If you follow me you might know that, immediately before this, I had watched a weird little gem of French cinema called Car Cemetery, a surreal punk rock "musical" mixing grimy, torturous and explicit sexual acts with messianic parable all while taking place in a post-apocalyptic junkyard. In my review of the movie I joked that it was "queerer than Cats." Not having seen Cats before and having an appreciation for strange and queer cinema, naturally I decided to put my money where my mouth is and challenge my assumptions on the matter. From the opening and throughout the first 10-15 minutes of the film I was engaged in an uncontrollable fit of hysterical laughter that seemed unstoppable despite my will to breathe. So early into the film, yet, had I already gone mad? How could this have been made with any intention other than to create a lovecraftian nightmare of fur and surreal landscapes. I believe the terror really set it about the time the Rebel Wilson Cat was concluding her number and began making unmistakeably suggestive petting motions. It was then I began to realized that all of these characters were trapped in an existential race towards death. The performers vying for the coveted "Jellical Choice" for their own reasons wanted to die. They were competing to prove which cat has suffered the most in whichever iteration of their 9 lives this was. Fear then turned to despair and however weird it was staring at Jennifer Hudson's face mapped onto a cartoonish cat body was not enough to distract me from the pain of existence that floated on every vocalization of "Memory." And then, just as it always does, the pain and suffering led to apathy. Maybe I too in some small way wanted to die, to move on from this nightmarish jest. Or maybe my hightened state of consciousness was just wearing off and I was getting bored. By the time the feline personification of Jennifer Hudson started floating off into the sunrise destined for reincarnation, I began foolishly searching for a deeper meaning to the whisical chaos of the film. Do cats experience God like humans are known to do? Does time exist as an infinite line or does it loop-de-loop over and over again until our astral bodies fade from existence. But alas the revelation in the form of Dame Judy Dench(s face on a cats body) staring into the camera and singing about addressing your cat with respect. A message which to me hearkens back to the theme of universal suffering, itself a strangely fitting echo of the words of the Great Buddha and the 4 Noble Truths, simplified to express an even more basic truth. We are all here in this reality together, and as we suffer and fight to mold our existence into something a little less distressing, we should always remember to treat all creatures with the respect they deserve. I shockingly rated this film 3 stars, because despite the unintentionally laughable moments, the uncomfortable character design, and all the many WTF moments, I still found myself in appreciation, if for nothing else, than the sheer insanity that resulted in this film. ...Oh yea, and the fact that it's queer as Fuuuuuck!

É, eu sei o que você está pensando... "como assim???" Apenas me escute Quando o trailer de Cats saiu, eu nao tive interesse nenhum nessa bomba, mas aí um dos meus melhores amigos disse que a gente ia ver no cinema. Eu disse a ele: "-Por que você quer fazer isso??? Esse filme claramente vai ser uma chacota, uma vergonha ridícula" "-Eu sei, você não quer muito conferir esse desastre ao vivo???" E de fato, eu não tive resposta pra essa fala, então, um dia depois do Natal fomos a uma vazia sala de cinema pra assistir um filme que já nasceu morto. E foi umas das experiências mais inesquecíveis de cinema na minha vida. Por ter ido sem nenhuma expectativa de que esse filme pudesse ser bom, eu fui capaz de me divertir bastante sem levar nada a sério. A lógica irrealista (e incoerente) de Cats faz com que literalmente qualquer coisa na cena possa ficar muito engraçada por simplesmente estar ali, é como estar vivenciando um delírio de alta definição. Eu ri absurdamente de várias cenas... mas o que é engraçado mesmo é que eu pude sentir um genuíno charme no meio de toda aquela esquisitice. Eu já reassisti Cats várias vezes e os primeiros 30 minutos realmente me entretém, porque são num ritmo muito dinâmico de música e dança que, se você puder desligar o senso crítico, vai só te carregando nessa gracinha de cenas que não tem absolutamente nenhuma história a não ser gatos cantando. Mais pro meio do filme, realmente começa a ficar enfadonho e cansativo, pois o filme começa a se levar a sério, e quando ele tenta se levar a sério aí é realmente só um desastre mesmo. Tecnicamente, é um filme que de fato merece todo o chapisco. O diretor foi um maníaco que quis fazer caprichos técnicos que dificultaram a vida de todos os profissionais que trabalharam na pós-produção do filme, então esse cara merece mesmo ser avacalhado e ter seu trabalho chamado de o pior filme de todos. E é realmente curioso pensar como nomes tao pesados toparam estar no elenco desse filme. Mas sendo muito sincero, assistir Cats no cinema me trouxe uma epifania de que eu me sentia tão envolvido por aquele filme que não importava de nada que ele fosse um desastre. A sua autenticidade ressoou em mim de uma forma que no final, eu quase me convenci de que era um filme bom. Estou frisando isso para que você entenda que eu não estou defendendo a qualidade de Cats. Estou apenas dizendo que não importa ele ser ruim Às vezes, nós deveríamos só assistir mais filmes ruins e nos entregar à liberdade de não esperar nada do que estamos assistindo. Praticar o exercício de apenas nos entregarmos na experiência de uma obra, e assim percebermos que talvez, um filme ruim também possa te oferecer uma coisa boa. Um filme ruim pode ser engraçado pra caralho. No pior dos casos você ainda vai treinar mais o seu senso crítico. Hoje em dia é tão fácil ser exigente e crítico com tudo, que eu sinto que a coisa mais saudável a se fazer seria realmente, não assistir todo filme do mundo esperando que ele seja bom, mas que seja pelo menos interessante. E isso vai de encontro a uma coisa que eu quero ressaltar: A MAIORIA DAS PESSOAS JULGA ESTE TIPO DE FILME SEM NEM TER SE DADO AO TRABALHO DE VER PRA FALAR MAL. A ESTAS PESSOAS O MEU DESPREZO QUER FALAR MAL???? ASSISTA E TENHA PROPRIEDADE PARA FALAR MAL Pois Cats é um filme horrível mesmo, mas se você se permitir aceitar que ele é horrível, pode talvez conseguir deixar ele te envolver numa experiência lúdica e engraçada, ao fim da qual você vai perceber que ele é um filme ruim de fato, mas nem tanto assim pra criar caso..... I really do love this movie more than I should. I know a lot of people find the visuals and some of the performances pretty detestable, and I understand that, but I think a lot of them are genuinely very good. The only truly awful performance is from Rebel Wilson, who manages to be intrusive in scenes dedicated to her. This is one of only two James Corden performances I defend, because I think he does a good job outside of the barge, where absolutely no one is doing their best work. It’s also fun to see the places where the visual style of the cats does work (mainly Old Deuteronomy and Gus) vs where it decidedly looks like a joke (think Macavity or Victoria). They seemingly removed a lot of the sexiness moving from the stage musical to Cats 2019, Id have to assume to appeal to as wide an audience as possible. Cats (1998) has a lot of the characters specifically play into things that are pretty widely considered hot, especially with someone like The Rum Tum Tugger being an amalgamation of Elvis and Bowie. There’s also this insane scene in the stage musical where they full body feel up Victoria for some reason. All of that has been removed and replaced with some light pawing and head nudges from some of the characters. The hottest thing in the movie is like, Taylor Swift cat doing cunty little dances or whatever.  Not to say this is either bad or good, just sort of interesting. I find this is inevitable when moving from sheer visual spectacle to like, trying to bring a coherent plot from cats. One thing I wasn’t too keen on watching these back to back was taking the songs from being sung about the cat by the rest of the Jellicles to being sung by the cat about themselves. It really goes from feeling like an introduction to these characters from a friendly face to being a railroading not dissimilar to a theme park. It also removes these ensembles that really are the heart and soul of Cats. Cats (1998) has so many moving bodies in every song and scene that the visual identity is never compromised. There’s never blank space if that makes sense. Cats 2019 eschews this in favor of taking on the styling of a 2010’s movie musical with all the various scenes. I’m just not certain it works. For as much as people whinge about the visual inconsistencies, be it size or fur or whatever I find it’s never really bothered me. The size being inconsistent is fine to me. I feel like people largely wouldn’t notice if it wasn’t pointed out to them. The biggest issue with the character design to me is their hands. They clearly don’t know how to give a Cat human hands and as such don’t even bother to try. It ends up being sort of distracting in a lot of scenes. Otherwise, which a few exceptions mentioned above, I actually found it to be unobtrusive after your brain has a second to adjust. Feels not dissimilar to the Navi from avatar to me. I love this movie dearly. Cats has always been THE peak musical to me. It’s got a little bit of everything and as such ends up feeling like this big silly romp. I love Skimbleshanks in this. I think his number in 2019 is maybe my favorite song across both variations (special mention to Growltiger’s Last Stand which I think also stands above) and I’m glad that the viewing populace tends to feel the same way. When I first started preaching about Cats 2019, nobody shared my sentiment that the film was good. Nowadays, it’s built a cult following especially amongst the online transgender crowd. It feels nice to find my people that way in much the same way Victoria does here.

Rebel Wilson and James Corden do improvisational comedy with all the ardor and skill of drama club kids whose families have just been taken hostage at gunpoint. Yet, everything else in this film has the feeling of watching a two hour cutaway gag from prime seasons of The Simpsons; it takes very little imagination to picture Troy McClure starring in this. When I saw this in theaters for the first time, I kept leaning over to my best friend and whispering, with unbridled exhilaration, "They made this into a movie!" Tom Hooper is not a talented director, which makes him perfect for this movie as a workmanlike, or even well made, version of this material would be forgetable to all but a handful of the most debased musical theater perverts. In Hooper's other pictures, he has a baseline level of competence more-or-less sufficient to overcome his penchant for deeply strange choices. Choices like like throwing dutch angles into his period prestige films-- or having the section of the John Adams miniseries where the title characeter goes to France mostly revolve around an elderly woman in clown make up jack off Benjamin Franklin in a tub (to be fair she could've also been milking his prostate; we don't get to see what's going on under the water). Here, however, the adulation Hooper received from his previous movies fried his brain; his hubris is archetypal. Every creative choice he makes big or small, is not merely off-- or sub-optimal-- they are objectively wrong. And that’s what makes Cats so special. There are many bad films, but they usually do some things right-- or alternatively they display a childlike lack of technical ability that reads as charming. Cats, inextricably, lands in neither category. It’s shaped like a movie. It has the bones, sinew, structure, and grammar of a movie in the way something like Birdemic or The Room never would. But despite its (mostly) quite talented cast, it's a series of wildly incorrect miscalculations that immediately begin to compound on one another and do not stop until the credits roll. Way better than Lesmis If cinema is about transporting audiences to places they’ve never been before, Cats wins before the opening number is even finished. While Les Misérables offers a grounded story of revolution, hardship, and redemption, Cats dares to ask a far more important question: what if an entire movie consisted of singing cats introducing themselves for two straight hours? Where Les Misérables is constrained by history, Cats is liberated by pure imagination. The film throws realism out the window and replaces it with giant furniture, mysterious feline lore, and an unwavering commitment to spectacle. Every scene feels like a dream you had after eating too much cheese at midnight. The music is another advantage. Les Misérables gives us heartbreaking ballads about suffering and sacrifice. Cats gives us songs about railway cats, magical cats, theatrical cats, and cats whose defining personality trait is simply being another cat. The thematic focus is admirable. Visually, Cats is impossible to ignore. Whether you find the digital fur groundbreaking, bewildering, or both, you will remember it. Years after watching, people still discuss it. That’s cultural impact. Most importantly, Cats understands entertainment. It doesn’t ask viewers to contemplate poverty, justice, or the human condition. It asks them to watch famous actors dance around as oversized cats. That level of confidence deserves respect. In conclusion, while Les Misérables may be a beloved adaptation of a literary masterpiece, Cats offers something much rarer: an experience that leaves audiences wondering what they just witnessed. And sometimes, that’s the true magic of cinema.
